extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public administration and political science; policymakers and historians interested in administrative systems and civil service reform
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style historical and analytical account of U.S. administrative systems, explaining principles (popular control, separation of powers), party roles, spoils system, civil service reform, and centralization vs. decentralization. Useful for learning criteria by which administrative arrangements are judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of popular control
rubrics_metrics.description: The framers based new state governments on the principle of popular control, making a complete break with past formal institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption of popular control necessitated elective officers and frequent elections; under this principle important officers are elected and serve short terms. This shapes expectations about accountability and the form of administrative institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective officers and frequent elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision was made for electing all important officers of government and for giving them short terms of office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent elections and elective offices were used to ensure popular control but produced decentralized administration and made state administrative supervision over executing officers difficult or impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers limiting legislative removal
rubrics_metrics.description: The adoption of the principle of the separation of powers made it impossible for the legislature to exercise any important power of control over executive officers through removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, the legislature's only practical recourse if dissatisfied was to regulate duties in detail and rely on courts to enforce; this structural limit affects how well the legislature can coordinate execution with policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed legislation as substitute for administrative supervision
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislatures attempted to achieve control by regulating in detail the duties of officers intrusted with execution of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed statutory regulation was used because direct administrative supervision was structurally difficult; but such detail can be impractical to enforce and can produce other problems (e.g., government by injunction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of judicial control
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts could take action only in cases of glaring disobedience and were hampered by juries reflecting local popular feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on courts to enforce detailed legislation is often unsatisfactory because judicial remedies are reactive, limited in scope, and influenced by local sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for coordination between expression and execution of the state's will
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordination between the functions of expressing and executing the will of the state had to be found because the governmental system could not provide it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without coordination, laws may not be effectively executed; institutional mechanisms — internal (administrative hierarchy) or extra-legal (political parties) — are required to secure harmony between policy-making and implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political party as the extra-legal coordinating institution
rubrics_metrics.description: The party organization took upon itself the burden of selecting both legislators and executive officers and thereby coordinated expression and execution of the state's will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties selected central and local officers, required party regularity, platforms, and candidate acceptance to ensure that elected officials would carry out agreed policies; this compensates for institutional separation of powers but has consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for party strength and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: The party organization had to be both strong and permanent to perform the coordination function effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strength is needed to bind individual officers to party platforms; permanence is required because staggered terms and numerous elections mean coordination cannot be achieved in a single election. Maintaining such organizations requires sustained resources and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Party regularity and discipline (platform acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Party regularity was prized: each candidate was supposed to stand upon a platform and formally accept it; individual candidates became subordinate to the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discipline reduces individual professions of faith and enables voters to rely on party platforms and records when electing many officers simultaneously or across large jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of material incentives for party managers
rubrics_metrics.description: Those engaged in party management cannot be expected to devote the required time and energy from purely disinterested motives; they must be paid or otherwise rewarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because party organization work is arduous and time-consuming, pecuniary rewards (salaries, offices) or extralegal means will be used to maintain party apparatus; this creates incentives shaping administrative appointments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation in office and extension of elective norms to appointive posts
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of rotation in office and treating appointive ministerial officers like elective ones (subject to change with party victory) became common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying rotation to ministerial positions was often justified by party needs rather than administrative necessity; it weakened continuity and institutional memory in administrative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spoils system definition and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: The spoils system subjected all officers, discretionary or ministerial, appointive or elective, to control of the political party as a means of coordinating politics and administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The spoils system arose from the perceived need to keep party organization strong; offices were regarded as rewards for party service, which served party cohesion but had administrative costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal faults of the spoils system
rubrics_metrics.description: The spoils system (1) seriously impaired administrative efficiency when applied to ministerial appointive officers; (2) aided formation of party machines that made the party an end rather than a means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As an anti-pattern, spoils lead to incompetent staffing of important positions and to parties organized to retain power rather than to express the public will; both outcomes degrade governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralization of national administration under the President
rubrics_metrics.description: The national administrative system embodied germs of administrative centralization, culminating in recognition of the President as head of the administrative system with power of appointment, removal, direction, and supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presidential removal and appointment powers and the development of departmental hierarchies allowed central direction, reducing the need to politicize lower-level officials to secure coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official hierarchy and supervisory appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of a recognized official hierarchy permitted heads of departments to reverse or modify decisions of inferior officers and for appeals to a superior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An administrative hierarchy fosters uniformity and discipline in execution; courts have upheld remedies (mandamus) forcing inferior officers to carry out superior decisions, strengthening central supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service reform via competitive examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Open competitive examinations were introduced (mid-19th century onward) to prevent incompetent men from entering the civil service and to restore administrative efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examinations were first applied to relatively minor ministerial positions and have been progressively extended (e.g., Civil Service Rules covering many positions). They are effective mainly for positions where technical fitness can be tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing removals for political reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent executive orders and rules recognize that a vast body of ministerial administrative officers shall be taken out of the control of parties and protected from removals for political reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and administrative steps to limit removals for partisan reasons are part of reform toward an administration whose functioning is free from political influence; enforcement and judicial remedies may be limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultimate objective: administration free from political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate object of civil service reform is recognition of a function of government whose discharge shall be free from the influences of politics, akin to administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitive exams and protections are means toward a broader public opinion and institutional change that demand selection and retention based on fitness rather than party service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological and social change necessitating centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase in administrative work, urbanization, and technological advances (railroads, telegraph, telephone) made decentralized systems unsuited and necessitated centralization of administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As administrative tasks grew more complex and interdependent, old decentralized elective-based systems failed; centralization and professionalization became practical responses to modern governance needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: government by injunction resulting from over-detailed statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive statutory detail (e.g., in prohibition laws) led legislatures to attempt enforcement via injunctions and contempt, producing 'government by injunction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legislatures try to force execution through detailed rules and judicial injunctions, execution may be inconsistent, lead to circumvention by local sentiment (juries), and prompt extra-legal coordination mechanisms (parties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsuitability of elective norms for ministerial officers with little discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the elective principle and rotation to ministerial appointive officers (with slight discretion) cannot be justified by the underlying principle and harms administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice was driven by party needs rather than theory; distinguishing administrative from political functions suggests many ministerial posts are better insulated from partisan turnover.
